newsitem.title: UK: German firm wins British drugstore chain.
newsitem.headline: German firm wins British drugstore chain.

text.p: German drug wholesaler and manufacturer Gehe AG clinched a tense, yearlong fight for control of British retail chain Lloyds Chemists Plc on Monday after outgunning rival Unichem Plc.

In the end, the superior financial firepower of Stuttgart-based Gehe -- which upped its cash bid for Lloyds on Friday to 525 pence ($8.79) per share from 500 pence ($8.37), putting the value of LLoyds at 684 million pounds ($1.15 billion) -- proved too much for Unichem.

The British company effectively admitted defeat Monday by refusing to raise its largely stock-based bid, hoping vainly that the promise of "potential rewards" from the combination of Lloyds with its own retail chain, Moss Chemists, would be strong enough to sway Lloyds' shareholders.
But by the end of the day Gehe, was able to claim control of 78 percent of Lloyds shares after Lloyds' board said it would recommend the German offer.

Unichem, which has around 30 percent of Britain's drug wholesale market, found its attempt to make itself a major player in the retail sector fatally undermined by the scepticism of its own shareholders. As concern grew about the earnings dilution of a Lloyds acquisition, the value of its own bid sank in line with its stock price.

Ironically, relief at the failure of the bid sparked a revaluation of Unichem on Monday, pushing its stock price up 13-1/2 pence (22.6 cents) to 269-1/2 pence ($4.51) by the market close and putting the value of its own offer for Lloyds within spitting distance of Gehe's winning bid.

Gehe's victory followed an exhausting yearlong tussle between the two companies, which began with an agreed 493 million pound ($825 million) offer from Unichem on Jan. 18, 1996. Gehe quickly responded with a 584 million-pound ($978 million) bid, eventually raising its offer to 650 million pounds ($1.09 billion) before the British government stepped in to consider the offers in March.

The government asked the Monopolies and Mergers' Commission to investigate the bids, deciding in July that both could go ahead on condition that a number of Lloyds' wholesale operations were sold off.

Gehe is now set to become a major player in British drugstores. Lloyds' 900-plus pharmacies will be added to around 360 owned by Gehe's existing British chain AAH, which means that it will overtake current market leader Boots Co. Plc's 1,200 outlets in terms of number of stores.
Unichem's own chain of Moss Chemists will remain well behind with around 470 outlets.
Analysts said both companies had hoped that the addition of the Lloyds chain would bring major benefits in supply, purchasing and advertising.
